what_its_for: Naloxegol is used to treat constipation caused by opioid pain medicines (such as morphine, oxycodone, or hydrocodone) in adults who have non-cancer pain. It works by blocking the effects of opioids in your gut so your bowels can move more normally, without reducing the pain relief you get from your opioid medicine.
how_to_take: Take naloxegol by mouth once every morning on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes BEFORE your first meal of the day. Swallow the tablet whole. If you have trouble swallowing it whole, you may crush the tablet, mix it with 4 ounces (half a cup) of water, and drink it right away. Do not take it with grapefruit juice or eat grapefruit while on this medicine. If you are taking certain other medicines (ask your pharmacist), you may need to adjust the timing — always check with your healthcare provider.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 25 mg (one tablet) once daily in the morning. If this dose causes bothersome side effects, your doctor may lower it to 12.5 mg once daily. Always take the dose your doctor prescribed. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but ONLY if it is still morning and you have not yet eaten. If it is already afternoon or close to your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose the following morning at your usual time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store naloxegol tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in a dry place away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it out of the reach of children and pets. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking this medicine, as it can increase the amount of drug in your body and raise your risk of side effects. Do not suddenly stop taking your opioid pain medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid taking naloxegol if your doctor has told you that you have a bowel blockage. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because many medicines can interact with naloxegol, especially certain antifungals (like ketoconazole), certain antibiotics (like clarithromycin), and some HIV medications.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek medical help RIGHT AWAY if you experience: severe stomach pain, cramping, or vomiting that does not go away; symptoms of opioid withdrawal such as sweating, chills, shaking, goosebumps, feeling anxious, runny nose, or yawning; a tear or hole in your stomach or intestines (signs include sudden severe stomach pain, fever, nausea, or vomiting — this is rare but serious); or if your constipation does not improve. Also call your doctor if you develop diarrhea that is severe or persistent.
when_it_works: Many people have their first bowel movement within the first day or two of starting naloxegol. You should notice regular improvement in your constipation within the first few days. If your symptoms do not improve after a few days, let your doctor know. Results can vary from person to person.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If you have moderate to severe kidney disease, your doctor may start you on a lower dose of 12.5 mg. Make sure your doctor knows about any kidney issues before starting this medicine. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine may cause opioid withdrawal in an unborn baby. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not known if naloxegol passes into breast milk, so discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Older adults: Naloxegol can be used in older adults, but they may be more sensitive to side effects. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: This medicine is NOT approved for use in children under 18 years of age.
